items.prompt: Explain why a business needs finance before it has made a single sale.
items.canonical_answer: Because the things that make a sale possible have to be paid for first. Premises and their deposit, equipment, the opening stock, registration and licence fees all fall due before any customer has been served, and rent, wages and power run from the first day while trade is still building. Trading income arrives only after all of that is in place, so the money has to come from somewhere else in the meantime.
marking_guidance: The reason must be given, not only a list: the spending happens before the trading income that would pay for it.
At least two named start-up outlays should appear - equipment, premises, opening stock, licence fees, or the running costs of the first months.
Credit the point that some start-up money buys time rather than an asset.

items.prompt: Nedu is opening a car wash in Rundu. Equipment and site preparation cost N$140 000, opening stock of chemicals N$12 000, and he expects to need N$30 000 for rent, wages and water over the first two months. He has N$95 000 of his own savings. Calculate how much finance he must raise from elsewhere, and explain what that money is buying.
items.canonical_answer:
The start-up need is N$140 000 of equipment and site preparation, N$12 000 of chemicals and N$30 000 of running costs - N$182 000 in all. Against his own N$182 000 - N$95 000 = N$87 000 has to be raised elsewhere.

What it buys is not one thing. N$140 000 buys assets Nedu keeps and uses for years. N$12 000 buys stock that will be used up and replaced within weeks. The N$30 000 buys neither: it buys time, covering the wages, rent and water of the months before enough cars are coming through to pay for them. The third is the one new owners most often leave out of the figure, and it is the one that decides whether the business survives long enough to become profitable.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use Nedu's own figures, not describe start-up costs in general.
Reasoning: the arithmetic must be shown, and the three kinds of spending distinguished because they are tied up for different lengths of time.
Conclusion: must reach N$87 000 and say what the money is for.

items.prompt: A bakery wins a contract to supply four supermarkets, which will roughly double its sales. Analyse why it may need finance even though the contract is profitable.
items.canonical_answer:
Start from the order of events. The bakery has to be able to produce the extra bread before it delivers any: a second oven, extra staff, more flour and packaging, perhaps a delivery vehicle. Every one of those is paid for in the weeks before the first supermarket delivery, so cash leaves the business first.

The supermarkets then buy on credit, because that is how supermarkets buy. The bread is delivered in week one and paid for perhaps sixty days later, so the bakery is carrying the cost of two months of doubled production before any of the new revenue reaches its bank account.

The effect is that the more successful the contract is, the larger the gap becomes, because a bigger order means more flour, more wages and more delivery cost carried for the same sixty days. Profitability does not close that gap: profit is recorded when the bread is delivered, while the cash arrives two months later.

So the consequence for the business is a demand for finance that rises with its own growth. If it cannot meet it, the result is not a lost profit but an inability to pay wages and suppliers in the meantime, which puts the contract itself at risk.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the chain must begin from the fact that capacity and materials are bought before the contract is delivered.
Mechanism: must explain how credit terms separate the delivery from the payment.
Consequence: must reach the effect that the need grows as the contract grows.
End point: the chain must land on the business's cash position and its ability to pay wages and suppliers, not stop at 'it needs money'.

context.situation: new supermarket supply contract doubling output

items.prompt: Explain how one large customer paying sixty days late can create a need for finance in a business that is trading profitably.
items.canonical_answer:
The business has already spent the money. Materials were bought, staff were paid and the job was delivered, so the cost has left the bank. The revenue is recorded as profit on delivery, but the money is now sitting in the customer's account for a further sixty days.

Meanwhile the business's own obligations keep their own dates. Wages fall due at the end of the month, the supplier's invoice at thirty days, the instalment on the vehicle on the same day as always. None of them moves because a customer is slow.

So a gap opens between money committed and money received, and it has to be filled from somewhere - from a cash reserve if the business has one, and from finance if it does not. The profit on the job is real and will arrive, but it will arrive after the dates on which the business has to pay.
marking_guidance: The mechanism must be traced, not asserted: costs paid out, revenue recorded, money delayed, obligations unchanged.
The answer must make clear that the profit is not in doubt - only its timing.
Credit any reference to the business's own payment dates being fixed.

items.prompt: A Tsumeb engineering firm needs N$300 000 to pay wages and buy steel for a large order that its customer will pay for in 60 days, and N$250 000 for a lathe it will use for eight years. Explain the difference between its short-term and long-term needs for finance.
items.canonical_answer: A short-term need is expected to be settled within about a year and comes from day-to-day trading; a long-term need lasts more than about a year and comes from spending on assets that will earn revenue over several years. The N$300 000 for wages and steel is a short-term need: the customer pays in 60 days and the money returns. The N$250 000 lathe is a long-term need: it earns its cost back over eight years. The boundary is how long the money stays tied up, not the size of the sum - here the larger amount is the short-term one.

items.prompt: Explain why a business tries to match the length of its finance to the length of the need that finance is paying for.
items.canonical_answer:
Because the repayments and the earnings have to arrive in the same order. Finance repayable in months against an asset that earns over years puts the repayments first: the business owes the money back long before the asset has produced it, so it must find the difference elsewhere every month, and an asset doing exactly what was expected of it still creates a shortfall.

The opposite mismatch wastes rather than strains. Finance repayable over ten years used to buy a month's stock leaves the business paying for goods that were sold and consumed years earlier, and carrying an obligation it gets nothing further from.

Matching removes both problems: the money is repaid roughly as the need it paid for produces the means to repay it.
marking_guidance: The reason must be developed in both directions - finance too short, and finance too long - because each fails differently.
The short mismatch must reach a named consequence: repayments due before the asset has earned them.
Credit any answer that identifies the principle as aligning repayment with the life of the need.

items.prompt: A fishing company in Walvis Bay is planning three things: a freezer vessel costing N$14 000 000 and expected to work for twenty years; N$900 000 of fuel and crew wages for the coming month; and N$2 100 000 to refit the processing line, which will then serve for eight years. Explain which of the three is a short-term need, and what that classification tells the company about the finance it should look for.
items.canonical_answer:
The N$900 000 of fuel and crew wages is the short-term need. It is spent and recovered inside the year, and it recurs every month as the catch is landed and sold. The vessel at N$14 000 000 and the refit at N$2 100 000 are long-term needs: both tie money up for many years before trading returns it.

The classification matters because it points to the shape of the finance rather than the amount. The N$900 000 needs finance that can be drawn and repaid as the month turns over, because the need itself appears and disappears each month. The other two need finance repayable across the working life of what it buys, so that the repayments and the earnings arrive in step.

Note what does not decide it. The N$900 000 is a large sum, larger than plenty of long-term needs elsewhere, and it is still short term because the money is not committed for long.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must sort the company's own three figures, not define the terms in the abstract.
Reasoning: the classification must be justified by how long each amount is tied up, because that is what separates the two.
Conclusion: must reach a statement about the kind of finance each need calls for.

items.prompt: A transport business buys a truck for N$960 000 and arranges finance repayable in full over twelve months, although the truck is expected to work for eight years. The truck is expected to add about N$25 000 a month to the business once fuel, driver and maintenance are paid. Analyse the effect of that financing choice on the business.
items.canonical_answer:
The capital repayment is N$960 000 / 12 = N$80 000 a month. The truck earns about N$25 000 a month after its running costs, so from the first month the truck falls short of its own repayment by N$80 000 - N$25 000 = N$55 000, and over the year that is N$55 000 x 12 = N$660 000 that has to come from somewhere else in the business.

From there the effects spread. That N$660 000 is money not available for fuel, wages and supplier payments, so the working capital of the rest of the business is drained to service one asset. If the shortfall is met by delaying suppliers, terms are likely to tighten and the following months get harder. If it cannot be met at all, the business may have to sell the truck, and a truck sold under pressure within its first year commonly fetches well below what was paid for it.

The point of the analysis is where the fault lies. The truck is not the problem: over eight years the same N$960 000 is N$960 000 / 96 = N$10 000 a month, which N$25 000 covers comfortably. The mismatch between a twelve-month repayment and an eight-year earning life is the problem.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the chain must begin from the monthly repayment set against what the truck actually earns.
Mechanism: must explain how the shortfall is transmitted to the rest of the business because the money has to come from working capital.
Consequence: must reach a named effect - supplier terms, a forced sale, or an inability to pay.
End point: must separate the asset from the financing, and reach the business's cash position rather than stopping at 'it is expensive'.

The furniture maker's N$40 000 profit counts the hotel's N$120 000 order as March revenue, but the hotel's money arrives in May, while the timber and wages for that order were paid in March. items.prompt: Explain how a business can report a profit for a month in which its bank balance fell.
items.canonical_answer:
Three movements pull the two figures apart, and any of them is enough on its own.

Sales made on credit count as revenue as soon as the goods are delivered, so they raise the profit for the month while the money is still with the customer. A month of strong credit sales adds profit and no cash at all.

Repaying borrowed money takes cash out but is not a cost of trading, so it reduces the bank balance while leaving the profit figure untouched.

Buying a non-current asset takes the cash in full on the day it is paid, while only part of its cost is charged against profit in each year the asset is used - so the bank falls by far more than the profit figure does.

Underneath all three is the same point: profit is measured when a sale is made and a cost incurred, and cash is measured when money moves.
marking_guidance: The mechanism must be traced through at least two of the three routes, because a single example does not show why the two figures diverge in general.
The answer must be explicit that profit is recorded on delivery and on the incurring of a cost, not on payment.
Credit an answer that notes the effect runs the other way as well.

items.prompt: In March, Etosha Fittings invoices N$260 000 of work on thirty-day credit and incurs costs of N$195 000, all of which it pays during March. It also receives N$150 000 from work invoiced in February and pays a N$40 000 instalment on money it borrowed last year. Calculate its profit for March and the change in its cash balance.

Profit = revenue - costs = N$260 000 - N$195 000 = N$65 000.

Cash received in March = N$150 000, from February's invoices. Cash paid out = N$195 000 of costs + N$40 000 instalment = N$235 000. The cash balance therefore falls: N$235 000 - N$150 000 = N$85 000.

So March produced N$65 000 of profit and a fall of N$85 000 in the bank. The March invoices count as revenue on delivery but are not due for another thirty days, and the N$40 000 instalment returns borrowed money rather than paying a cost of trading, so it takes cash without reducing profit.

items.prompt: A learner writes that a business with N$200 000 in the bank must have made a profit of N$200 000. Identify the error and correct it.
items.canonical_answer:
The error is treating the bank balance as the profit figure. They are measured on different bases and over different things.

The N$200 000 is a balance at a moment in time and says nothing about how it got there. It might include money owed to suppliers that has not yet been paid out, the proceeds of selling a vehicle, or finance recently received - and none of those is revenue. Meanwhile the profit of the period could be far higher, if much of what was sold has not yet been paid for, or negative, because a business can be losing money and still hold cash for a while.

The correction: profit is revenue minus the costs of earning it over a period, recorded when the sale is made and the cost incurred. Cash is what is held now.
marking_guidance: The error must be named, not merely contradicted.
The correction must explain the different basis of the two figures.
An example of cash arriving without revenue - an asset sale or new finance - should appear.

items.prompt: Oshakati Interiors has just reported its best year for profit and has told its staff so. The same week it asked its main fabric supplier for an extra thirty days to pay. Explain how both can be true at the same time.
items.canonical_answer:
Profit measures the year's trading; the supplier has to be paid on a particular Friday. A business fitting out offices sells largely on credit, so a record year of profit can consist mostly of invoices delivered and recorded as revenue but not yet collected. The fabric that went into those jobs, however, was bought and paid for months ago.

A strong year also tends to make this worse rather than better, because more work means more fabric, more wages and more money committed before the customers pay. Add any assets bought during the year - a van, a cutting table - which take cash in full but are charged against profit slowly, and the bank balance can be at its tightest in the year the profit is at its highest.

So the request to the supplier is not an admission that the reported profit was wrong. It is a statement about when the money arrives.

items.prompt: Explain why the personal assets of a sole trader may be reached when the business cannot pay its debts.
items.canonical_answer:
Because a sole trader has unlimited liability. In law the owner and the business are not separate persons, so the debts the business runs up are the owner's own debts, not the debts of something standing between the owner and the creditors.

The consequence is that creditors who cannot be paid from what the business holds may pursue the owner personally, and assets held outside the business - a house, a vehicle, savings - may be sold to meet the shortfall. The loss is not limited to the amount the owner put in.
marking_guidance: The reason must be unlimited liability, stated as the absence of legal separation between owner and business.
The answer must reach the consequence that assets outside the business may be used.

items.prompt: Selma runs a catering business as a sole trader. It owes N$340 000 to suppliers and the bank, and its equipment and stock would raise about N$110 000 if sold. Explain what bankruptcy would mean for Selma in this situation.

Selling everything the business holds leaves a shortfall of N$340 000 - N$110 000 = N$230 000. Because Selma is a sole trader with unlimited liability, that N$230 000 is not a debt of a separate company that stops when the company's assets run out. It is her own debt.

In bankruptcy the declaration is made against Selma rather than against the catering business. Control of her assets passes to an appointed official; the business equipment and stock are sold, and so may assets she holds outside the business - a vehicle, savings, in some cases a house - until the creditors have been paid as far as the assets allow, in the order the law sets.

The consequences also outlast the business. Restrictions that follow a bankruptcy declaration, such as limits on borrowing or on holding certain offices, attach to Selma personally and remain when the catering business has gone.

items.prompt: Analyse how a shortage of finance in a sole trader's business can end in the owner being declared bankrupt.
items.canonical_answer:
The chain starts at a single missed payment, not at a loss. An amount falls due - a supplier's invoice, the wage bill - and the bank balance will not cover it.

What happens next makes the next month harder rather than easier. A supplier who has not been paid has its own money tied up and is likely to want cash before supplying again, so stock that used to arrive on credit must now be paid for up front, which takes more money rather than less. Staff whose wages are late begin to leave. Customers who hear that deliveries are slipping place their orders elsewhere, so the revenue that would have relieved the shortage falls.

Each step removes some of the finance that would have solved the problem at the step before, so the shortage grows. Eventually a creditor stops waiting and goes to court to recover what it is owed.

The last link is the one that makes it personal. Because a sole trader has unlimited liability, the business's debts are the owner's own debts, so the claim does not stop when the business's assets are exhausted. It continues against the owner, and where the owner cannot meet it either, the outcome is a declaration of bankruptcy against the person rather than the closing of a company.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the chain must begin from an inability to pay an amount that has fallen due, given that the business may still be profitable.
Mechanism: must show why the shortage feeds itself, because each step removes finance.
Consequence: must reach legal action by a creditor.
End point: must connect unlimited liability to the outcome for the owner, so the chain ends on survival of the owner's personal position and not only of the business.

items.prompt: Explain what happens to a company's assets, its creditors and its shareholders when the company is liquidated.
items.canonical_answer:
The assets are taken into the control of an appointed liquidator and sold, with the aim of raising as much as possible from them.

The creditors are paid out of the proceeds in an order set by law. Where the proceeds are not enough to pay them all, those further down the order receive part of what they are owed, or nothing.

The shareholders rank last. They receive anything left after every creditor has been paid, which in an insolvent liquidation is commonly nothing. Their loss is limited to what they invested, because the company has limited liability and their personal assets are not normally reached - unless a shareholder has given a personal guarantee for a company debt, which is a separate obligation of their own.

At the end of the process the company ceases to exist.
marking_guidance: All three parties must be covered - assets, creditors, shareholders.
The order of payment must be stated, with shareholders last.
Credit the limited liability point and the exception where a personal guarantee has been given.

items.prompt: Two Namibian companies are being wound up: one after a supplier it owes N$2 million applied to the court, the other because its owners are retiring and closing a business that can pay all its debts. items.canonical_answer: Compulsory liquidation is forced on a company from outside, typically after an unpaid creditor applies to a court; voluntary liquidation is begun by the company itself, through its shareholders. items.prompt: A private limited company goes into liquidation owing N$2 400 000. Selling everything it owns raises N$1 500 000. Explain what this means for its creditors and for its shareholders.
items.canonical_answer:
There is a shortfall of N$2 400 000 - N$1 500 000 = N$900 000, so the creditors cannot all be paid in full. The N$1 500 000 is distributed among them in the order the law sets, which means creditors near the front may be paid in full while those further back receive part of what they are owed, or nothing. The unpaid N$900 000 is not recoverable from the shareholders, because the claims stop at the company's own assets.

For the shareholders, nothing is left. They rank after every creditor, and here the creditors have not even been covered, so no distribution reaches them. Their loss is the money they put into the company, and it is limited to that: limited liability means their personal assets are not normally reached to meet the N$900 000.

The exception is worth naming, because it is common in a small company. Where a shareholder or director personally guaranteed one of the company's debts - an overdraft, a supplier account - that guarantee is their own obligation and can still be enforced against them even though the company has been wound up.

Reasoning: the treatment of creditors and shareholders must be justified by the order of payment and by limited liability.
Conclusion: must state clearly what each group receives, and name the personal guarantee exception.

items.prompt: Explain why the creditors of a struggling company may do better from administration than from immediate liquidation.
items.canonical_answer:
Because a business sold as a working whole is generally worth more than the same assets sold separately. A bakery with staff, recipes, a delivery round and a supermarket contract has a value as a going concern; broken up, it is a set of second-hand ovens and a van, and second-hand equipment sold under pressure tends to fetch a fraction of what it cost.

Administration is what makes that sale possible, and the reason is time. While the company is in administration it normally has protection from creditors enforcing their claims, so the business is not dismantled piece by piece while a plan is being made. With that space the administrator can look for a buyer, renegotiate what is owed, or close the loss-making parts and keep the rest.

The larger realisation is then shared among the same creditors, so the reason they may favour it is arithmetic rather than sentiment. It is not a certainty: the rescue may fail, the administrator's costs come out of the same money, and a further period of trading can add to the losses, in which case liquidation follows anyway and less is left than there would have been.
marking_guidance: The reason must be developed to the point of why a going concern is worth more, because that is what the creditors gain.
The role of protection from enforcement must appear as the mechanism that makes the attempt possible.
The answer must not present the better outcome as certain; the risk that the attempt fails and costs money must be acknowledged.

items.prompt: A manufacturer has a full order book but its bank has withdrawn the overdraft, so it cannot pay wages next week. Evaluate whether administration is likely to produce a better outcome for its creditors than immediate liquidation.
items.canonical_answer:
On balance administration is the better course here, and the reason is the order book. A full order book is a realisable asset in a way that idle machinery is not: a buyer will pay for a factory with customers attached, and the same machinery sold separately at auction fetches far less. Administration is the procedure that keeps the order book alive long enough to be sold, because the protection from creditors enforcing their claims stops the business being taken apart while an administrator looks for a buyer or renegotiates the debts.

The decisive criterion is whether the business is losing money on the work it is doing. If the orders are profitable and the failure is one of cash - the overdraft withdrawn, not the products unsaleable - then trading on under an administrator adds value, and more is left for the creditors at the end of it. If the orders were taken at prices below cost, every week of further trading destroys value, and the protection merely delays a smaller distribution.

The strongest argument the other way is cost and risk. Administration is not free: the administrator's fees come out of the same money the creditors would otherwise share, a rescue that fails ends in liquidation anyway, and the months in between can add new debts. Creditors who would have been paid in full from an immediate sale can be worse off for having waited.

The judgement therefore depends on two things that have to be checked rather than assumed: whether the orders are profitable at the prices agreed, and whether a buyer for the business is realistically available. Where either is absent, the recommendation reverses and immediate liquidation is the better course.

items.prompt: Explain why a business needs working capital even when it is trading profitably.
items.canonical_answer:
Because profit and payment dates are not the same thing. A business pays for stock and labour before it sells, and where it sells on credit it is paid again later still, so money leaves the business well before it comes back. A retailer that pays its supplier on day 30, sells the goods on day 45 and is paid on day 75 has parted with money for 45 days.

Working capital is what covers that gap. Its purpose is to let the business meet its obligations on the day they fall due, rather than on the day its customers get round to paying. Profitability does not remove the gap - a profitable business that grows will usually widen it, because more trade means more stock and wages carried for the same number of days.

items.prompt: Analyse what happens to a retailer that allows its working capital to fall too low.
items.canonical_answer:
Begin at the first missed date. The retailer cannot pay a supplier when the invoice falls due, so it pays late.

The supplier responds to protect its own position: terms are tightened, or payment is required with the order. That is the step that makes the problem worse rather than better, because stock which used to arrive on thirty days' credit now has to be paid for before it reaches the shelf. The business needs more working capital than before, at the moment it has least.

From there the effects multiply. Discounts for prompt payment are lost, so the cost of goods rises. If wages are paid late, staff leave, and a shop short of staff sells less. To raise cash quickly the retailer may cut prices on stock it holds, which brings money in but throws away the margin the stock was carrying - so the next round of buying is funded from less.

Each step leaves less money for the month after, which is why a working capital shortage rarely stays the size it started. The consequence for the business is that survival, not profit, becomes the issue: the shop can be selling goods at a profit on every sale and still reach a date on which it cannot pay, which is the point at which a creditor may act.

Mechanism: must show why the supplier's response increases the working capital requirement.
Consequence: at least two further named effects - lost discounts, staff leaving, margin given away.
End point: must reach the business's survival and cash position, not stop at 'it has less money'.

items.prompt: Explain what it costs a business to hold much more working capital than it needs.
items.canonical_answer:
The cost is real but quiet, because nothing goes wrong on any particular day. Money held in inventory and in unpaid customer accounts earns nothing while it sits there, and it is money the business has already spent. A wholesaler holding N$410 000 of stock against purchases of about N$200 000 a month is carrying roughly two months of selling on its shelves; that sum could instead have paid down an overdraft it is paying interest on, bought a second delivery vehicle, or funded a marketing push - so the cost is the best of the things it is not doing.

Inventory carries a second cost on top of that, because stock held a long time may be damaged, go out of fashion or pass its date, in which case the money is not merely idle but lost. Money owed by customers carries its own version: the longer an account is outstanding, the larger the chance it is not collected at all.

So the aim is not the largest possible working capital. It is enough to meet what falls due, with as little as possible tied up beyond that.

items.prompt: Identify, in order, the stages a business works through to manage the money its credit customers owe it.
items.canonical_answer:
First, before any credit is given: check the customer. Trade references, how long the customer has traded and its payment record are the data to start from, and a new account is opened with a limit that rises as the customer proves reliable.

Second, set the terms and make sure the customer knows them. The payment period goes on the order and is repeated on the invoice, and it is applied consistently rather than mentioned only once an account is late.

Third, invoice promptly and accurately. The credit period does not begin until the invoice is issued, so an invoice sent a fortnight late gives away a fortnight of credit, and a wrong invoice gives the customer a reason to hold the whole amount while it is queried.

Fourth, monitor. A schedule showing how long each account has been outstanding is the working document, and it decides which accounts are chased first.

Fifth, chase what is overdue, early and by agreement, which generally recovers more than a demand made months later.

Finish with the decision the schedule forces on persistent late payers: tighten their terms, require payment with order, or decline further work. What the business has at the end of the sequence is a shorter average collection period and fewer accounts that are not collected at all - bought at the price of some sales it chose not to make.

items.prompt: Otavi Supplies is owed N$250 000 by customers who take about sixty days to pay. It offers 2.5% off for payment within ten days and expects the customers owing N$150 000 to take it, bringing that money in about fifty days - roughly 1.6 months - earlier. items.canonical_answer:
Cost of the discount = N$150 000 x 0.025 = N$3 750.

Cash actually received = N$150 000 - N$3 750 = N$146 250. Overdraft interest on that sum runs at N$146 250 x 0.012 = N$1 755 a month, so the interest saved by having it 1.6 months early is N$1 755 x 1.6 = N$2 808.

Net effect = N$3 750 - N$2 808 = N$942. Measured on interest alone the offer costs Otavi about N$942 more than it saves.

That means the discount is not worth offering for the sake of the interest. It could still be worth offering for a reason the calculation does not price - if Otavi is at its overdraft limit and needs the cash to pay wages, or if some of the N$150 000 would eventually not have been collected at all.

items.prompt: Explain why a business that could pay a supplier on day ten often waits until day thirty, when the agreed terms allow it.
items.canonical_answer:
Because the credit period is finance, and it costs nothing. For the twenty days between day ten and day thirty the business is holding money that would otherwise have left it, and it can use that money to pay wages, buy more stock or keep an overdraft smaller than it would otherwise be. Paying on day ten gives away twenty days of interest-free finance and receives nothing in return.

The effect is larger than it looks, because it repeats. A business buying every month is holding roughly twenty days of purchases at all times, so the saving is not a one-off but a permanent reduction in the working capital it has to find from elsewhere.

There are reasons to pay earlier, and they are specific rather than habitual: a discount for early settlement large enough to beat the value of holding the money, or a supplier relationship the business wants to strengthen. Waiting past day thirty is a different matter again, because the terms no longer permit it.

items.prompt: A manufacturer sells N$1 200 000 a month on credit and its customers take an average of seventy days to pay. Analyse the effect on the business of getting that average down to forty-five days.
items.canonical_answer:
Start with what a day of credit costs. Credit sales of N$1 200 000 / 30 = N$40 000 a day, so every day of average collection period ties up N$40 000 of the manufacturer's money. Cutting the average by twenty-five days releases 25 x N$40 000 = N$1 000 000 of cash, once the shorter period has worked through.

That million does not appear as extra profit, and saying so is the point of the analysis. It is money the business had already earned and was waiting for. What changes is what it can do: pay down an overdraft and save the interest, buy raw material in larger and cheaper quantities, or stop relying on stretching its own suppliers. The working capital the business must find from elsewhere falls by the same N$1 000 000.

The chain has a second half, though, and it runs the other way. The average comes down through tighter credit limits, firmer chasing and shorter terms, and each of those can cost a sale. If customers with a choice of supplier move to one offering seventy days, the lost contribution can outweigh the interest saved on the released cash.

So the effect on the business is a large, one-off improvement in cash and a permanent reduction in its working capital requirement, set against a risk to revenue that depends on what competing suppliers offer.

items.prompt: A small builders' merchant finds that a third of the money owed to it is more than sixty days overdue. Evaluate whether it should tighten the credit it gives its customers.
items.canonical_answer:
It should tighten, but selectively rather than across the board. A third of the debt more than sixty days overdue is not a timing wobble; it is a third of the money the business has already spent on timber and cement sitting in other people's businesses, and a merchant of this size cannot fund that indefinitely.

The decisive criterion is which customers the overdue debt belongs to. If it is concentrated in a few contractors, the answer is to act on those accounts - hold deliveries, require payment with order, set a firm limit - and leave everyone else alone, because the cost of tightening falls only where the problem is. If instead the lateness is spread evenly across the book, the terms themselves are wrong for the trade the merchant is in, and a general change is justified.

The strongest argument against tightening is that credit is part of what the merchant sells. Contractors are paid in stages by their own clients and buy where the terms let them work; a merchant that demands cash while the yard down the road offers thirty days may lose the customer and the debt together, and the contribution lost on those sales can exceed the money recovered.

So the judgement is conditional on two things the merchant can find out: whether the overdue debt is concentrated or general, and what competing merchants are offering. Where it is concentrated, tighten those accounts and keep the rest. Where the book is generally late and competitors are no more generous, tighten the terms for everyone. Where competitors are markedly more generous, the better route is firmer collection - prompt invoicing, a schedule of overdue accounts, early contact - rather than harder terms, because that recovers cash without giving the sales away.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a recommendation is required, and it must be more specific than 'it depends'.
Context: the argument must rest on this merchant's own position - a third of the book more than sixty days overdue, and contractors as customers.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be whether the overdue debt is concentrated in a few accounts or spread across the book.
Counterargument: must make the case that credit is part of what a builders' merchant sells and that tightening can cost the sale.
Condition: must name what would change the recommendation, including what competing merchants offer.

items.prompt: Grootfontein Motors is short of cash this month. Its accountant suggests paying suppliers forty-five days after delivery instead of the thirty days agreed. Explain what this would do for the business and what it risks.
items.canonical_answer:
What it does is straightforward. Fifteen extra days of supplier credit is fifteen days in which money stays in Grootfontein's account instead of leaving it, so the working capital it has to find from elsewhere falls by roughly fifteen days of purchases. For a business short of cash this month, that is immediate relief and it costs no interest.

What it risks is the difference between using a credit period and exceeding one. Thirty days was agreed; forty-five was not. A parts supplier whose money is late may shorten the terms to fifteen days, ask for payment with order, withdraw a prompt-payment discount, or move Grootfontein down the delivery list - and a garage that cannot get parts on credit, or waits longer for them, has a worse problem than the one it was solving, because cars sit unrepaired and customers go elsewhere.

The risk is larger where the business depends on one supplier for a part it cannot buy elsewhere. So the sensible version of the accountant's suggestion is to ask the supplier for forty-five day terms rather than simply taking them, and to make sure the collection of what Grootfontein's own customers owe is as tight as it can be first.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use Grootfontein's own situation - agreed thirty-day terms and a short-term cash problem.
Reasoning: the benefit must be explained as free finance, and the risk explained because the supplier has not agreed to the longer period.
Conclusion: must reach a clear position on what the business should do, including asking rather than taking.

The year's insurance and the replacement tyre are revenue expenditure: they keep the van doing what it already did and are used up within the period. So the bank balance falls by N$644 000 while the month's reported costs are N$99 000, because the cost of the machine and the extension is spread across the years in which they are used.

items.prompt: Explain how two businesses that spend exactly the same cash in a month can report very different profits for that month.
items.canonical_answer:
Because what the money was spent on decides how much of it is charged against that month.

A business whose N$600 000 went on wages, fuel and raw materials has spent it on revenue expenditure, which is used up inside the month and is charged in full against the month's profit. The reported cost is N$600 000.

A business whose N$600 000 went on a machine has spent it on capital expenditure. The asset will be used across several years, so its cost is spread over those years rather than landing on the month of purchase, and only a part of it is charged against this month's profit. The reported cost is a fraction of the cash.

The cash column is identical in both: N$600 000 has left each bank account. The profit column is not, and neither business is misrepresenting anything - they are answering the question 'what did this month's trading cost?' rather than 'what did we pay out?'
marking_guidance: The mechanism must be traced through the treatment of each kind of spending, not asserted.
The answer must state that revenue expenditure is charged in full in the period, because that is the source of the difference.
Credit an answer that keeps the cash effect identical while the profit effect differs.

items.prompt: A learner classifies a N$480 000 factory roof repair as capital expenditure because the sum is large, and a N$1 200 filing cabinet as revenue expenditure because the sum is small. Identify the error and correct it.
items.canonical_answer:
The error is sorting expenditure by the size of the amount. Size is not the test.

The test is what is bought and how long it will be used. Repairing a roof restores the factory to the condition it was already supposed to be in; it does not add a capability or create a new asset, so it is revenue expenditure however large the bill. The filing cabinet is an item the business will keep and use for years, so in principle it is capital expenditure however small the price.

One practical qualification belongs with the correction: many businesses set a monetary threshold below which small long-lived items are charged as running costs, because tracking them separately costs more than it is worth. That is a convention of convenience, not a different definition, and the underlying test stays the same.
marking_guidance: The error must be named as classification by size.
Both examples must be reclassified correctly with the reason for each.
The threshold convention may be credited, provided it is presented as a practical convention rather than as the definition.

items.prompt: Analyse why the distinction between capital and revenue expenditure matters to a business deciding what kind of finance to raise.
items.canonical_answer:
Start from what each kind of spending does to the money. Capital expenditure puts cash into an asset that will be used for years, so the money is committed for years and comes back only as the asset is used to earn. Revenue expenditure is spent and recovered inside the period: the wages and diesel of this month are recovered when this month's customers pay.

That difference is exactly the difference between a long-term and a short-term need for finance, so the classification of the spending settles the classification of the need. From there the matching principle follows: finance should be repayable over a period similar to the life of the need it pays for.

The consequence of getting it wrong runs in both directions. A truck financed over twelve months when it earns over eight years produces repayments far ahead of the earnings, and the difference is taken out of the working capital that was supposed to fund the diesel and the wages - so the business is short of money for trading because of the way an asset was paid for. Financing a month's raw material over ten years leaves the business paying long after the material has been sold.

So the effect on the business is direct: the capital-and-revenue split is what tells it which of its needs are long term, and therefore which kind of finance to go looking for.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the chain must begin from how long each kind of spending ties money up.
Mechanism: must link the classification to the short-term or long-term nature of the need, because that is what connects it to finance.
Consequence: must reach the matching principle and at least one named result of a mismatch.
End point: must land on the business's own decision about what finance to raise.

items.prompt: A restaurant in Swakopmund spends N$70 000 replacing broken chairs with identical ones, N$45 000 building a new outdoor deck, and N$18 000 on a deep clean of the kitchen. Its owner says that because the total is N$133 000 of cash, profit for the month will fall by N$133 000. Explain whether the owner is right.
items.canonical_answer:
The owner is right about the cash and wrong about the profit.

The deck at N$45 000 is capital expenditure: it is a structure the restaurant will use for years, and it gives the business seating it did not have. Its cost is spread across the years it is used, so only a small part of it is charged against this month. The deep clean at N$18 000 is revenue expenditure - it is used up at once and restores nothing beyond the condition the kitchen was already meant to be in. The chairs at N$70 000 are the interesting case: they are replacements for identical items, but they are still assets the restaurant will keep and use for years, so they are capital expenditure too. Replacing an asset is not the same as repairing one.

So the spending charged against this month's profit is the N$18 000 deep clean, plus a part of the cost of the chairs and the deck. Profit falls by far less than N$133 000.

The cash is a different matter, and the owner should not take comfort from the profit figure: N$133 000 has left the bank this month whatever the profit statement shows, and the wages still have to be paid at the end of it.
marking_guidance: Context: each of the restaurant's three items must be classified individually, using its own facts.
Reasoning: the chairs must be treated as replacement of an asset rather than repair, because that is the point the owner has missed.

items.prompt: Explain why a business can be pushed into a formal insolvency procedure even though the products it sells are profitable.
items.canonical_answer:
Because insolvency procedures begin at an unpaid amount, not at a loss. The reason a creditor goes to court is that money due on a particular date was not paid, and a profitable business reaches that date through late-paying customers, stock bought too far ahead, or growth that has outrun the finance behind it.

What then happens makes the position worse rather than better. Suppliers who have not been paid are likely to want cash before supplying again, so stock that used to arrive on credit must be paid for before it is sold; staff whose wages are late begin to leave; and customers who hear that deliveries are slipping move their orders. Each step removes some of the finance that would have solved the problem at the step before, so the shortage grows while the margin on every sale stays exactly as healthy as it was.

At the end of that sequence a creditor stops waiting. Which procedure follows depends on what the business is: bankruptcy where the debts are an individual owner's own, liquidation where a company is to be wound up, administration where a rescue is to be attempted.
marking_guidance: The reason must separate profitability from the ability to pay on a date, because that is the whole answer.
The self-reinforcing part of the sequence should be developed, not merely asserted.
Credit an answer that names which procedure follows for which kind of business.

items.prompt: A development agency lends to new businesses in northern Namibia and asks every applicant the same question. For each of the three stages - starting up, growing and surviving - identify one reason the business will need finance and whether that need is short term or long term, and explain what decides which it is. Answer as an applicant running a small poultry farm.
items.canonical_answer:
**Starting up.** The farm needs housing, feeders, water lines and the first batch of chicks before a single bird can be sold. The sheds and equipment are a long-term need: they are used for years, so the money stays tied up for years. The first batch of feed is not - it is consumed and recovered within weeks, so it is a short-term need even though it is bought at the same moment.

**Growing.** Adding a second shed means paying for the building, more chicks and more feed before any of the extra birds are sold, and if the farm supplies shops on credit the money arrives later still. The shed is a long-term need; the extra feed and labour carried in the meantime are short term, and they grow as fast as the flock does.

**Surviving.** A disease outbreak, a feed price rise, or a supermarket paying sixty days late all demand money at a moment when trading has not produced it. These are short-term needs: they are one-off gaps to be bridged, not assets to be bought.

**What decides it.** Not the size of the amount. A month's feed bill can be larger than a shed and is still short term. What decides it is how long the money stays tied up before trading returns it - weeks for feed, years for a shed. That is what the agency needs to know, because finance should be repayable over a period similar to the life of the need it pays for.
marking_guidance: State the point for each stage plainly before developing it.
Give the reason finance is needed at each stage - what the money buys and why trading has not yet provided it.
Use the context: each of the three answers must be about the poultry farm, not about businesses in general.
The classification must turn on how long the money is committed, and the answer must say so explicitly.

items.prompt: Rehoboth Paints sells N$900 000 a month, all on credit, and its customers take an average of sixty days to pay. At month end it holds inventory of N$640 000, is owed N$1 800 000 by customers and has N$40 000 in the bank; it owes suppliers N$520 000, has an overdraft of N$380 000 and owes N$90 000 in tax. The overdraft is at its limit. The owner is considering offering customers 2% off for payment within fifteen days, which she expects half the receivables to take. Calculate the working capital, calculate the cost of the discount on that half, and evaluate whether she should offer it.
items.canonical_answer:
Current assets: inventory N$640 000, receivables N$1 800 000 and cash N$40 000 - N$2 480 000 in total. Current liabilities: payables N$520 000, overdraft N$380 000 and tax N$90 000 - N$990 000 in total. Working capital = N$2 480 000 - N$990 000 = N$1 490 000.

Half the receivables is N$1 800 000 / 2 = N$900 000. The discount on that is N$900 000 x 0.02 = N$18 000, and the cash it brings in is N$900 000 - N$18 000 = N$882 000, arriving about forty-five days early.

Judgement: she should offer it. The decisive criterion is not the arithmetic of the discount but the state of the overdraft. Working capital of N$1 490 000 looks healthy until it is read: N$1 800 000 of it is money in other people's businesses and only N$40 000 is cash, against an overdraft already at its limit. Rehoboth has no capacity left to absorb a late payment, and N$18 000 is a small price for N$882 000 of cash and for the headroom it creates.

The strongest argument against is that the discount is permanent and the problem may not be. Every month the offer runs it costs N$18 000, roughly N$216 000 a year if half the book keeps taking it, and that is a real reduction in margin bought to fix a position that firmer collection might fix for nothing. Sixty days average on a business selling to trade customers is slow, and prompt invoicing and a schedule of overdue accounts cost less than 2% of revenue.

So the recommendation is conditional and has a time limit: offer it now, because the overdraft leaves no alternative source of short-term cash, and review it once collection has been tightened. If the bank were willing to extend the limit, or if the slow payment turned out to be concentrated in a few accounts that could be chased directly, the answer reverses and the discount should not be offered.

Judgement: a recommendation is required, not a presentation of both sides.
Context: the recommendation must rest on Rehoboth's own position - the overdraft at its limit and the composition of its current assets.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be the absence of any other source of short-term cash, not the size of the discount.
Counterargument: must address the permanence and annual cost of the discount against the cheaper alternative of firmer collection.
Condition: must name what would reverse the recommendation.

items.prompt: Plan an answer to: Namib Timber has reported rising profits for three years and its owner says that a profitable business does not need to worry about working capital. Evaluate that view.
items.canonical_answer:
Judgement to reach: the view is wrong, and it is most wrong for a business in exactly Namib Timber's position - profitable and growing.

Paragraph 1 - the two figures measure different things. Profit is revenue minus the costs of earning it, recorded when a sale is made and a cost incurred. Cash is what the business holds now. A timber merchant selling on credit records the profit on delivery and waits sixty days for the money.

Paragraph 2 - the mechanism by which growth makes it worse. Rising sales mean more timber bought, more wages paid and more money owed by customers, all carried before the customers pay. So the faster Namib Timber grows, the more working capital it needs, and three years of rising profit is three years of a widening gap.

Paragraph 3 - what a working capital figure does and does not show. It is current assets minus current liabilities, and in a merchant most of the current assets are stock in the yard and invoices not yet due. A positive figure does not mean the wage bill can be met on Friday.

Paragraph 4 - the consequence, traced. A missed payment brings tighter supplier terms, so stock must be paid for before it is sold, which needs more working capital at the moment there is least; discounts are lost, staff leave, and the business can reach a date on which a creditor acts - while every sale it makes is still profitable.

Paragraph 5 - the strongest case for the owner's view, stated properly. Sustained profit does generate cash eventually, and a profitable business with a record of rising profit is in a better position to arrange finance than an unprofitable one, so profitability reduces the chance that a shortage becomes fatal.

Judgement and condition: reject the view. Profit answers a different question from the one working capital answers, and the risk is largest in the growing, profitable business the owner is describing. The one situation in which the owner would be nearer right is a business paid in cash at the point of sale and holding little stock, where the gap between paying and being paid is close to nothing - which is not what Namib Timber is.
marking_guidance: A plan, not an essay: the structure and the point reached in each paragraph are what is assessed.
Judgement: the plan must show where the recommendation is reached and what it is.
Context: the plan must use Namib Timber's own facts - three years of rising profit, a credit-selling timber merchant.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be that profit and cash answer different questions, and that growth widens the gap.
Counterargument: the best case for the owner's view must be made, not dismissed.
Condition: must end on the circumstances in which the view would be closer to right.

items.prompt: Two Namibian businesses fail in the same month. Kavango Crafts is a sole trader owing N$410 000, with business assets worth about N$90 000. Erongo Engineering is a private limited company owing N$6 200 000, with plant worth about N$2 000 000, forty skilled staff and two long-term contracts with mines. Analyse which formal procedure each is likely to face, and evaluate what the owners of Erongo Engineering should do.
items.canonical_answer:
**Kavango Crafts.** Selling everything the business holds leaves N$410 000 - N$90 000 = N$320 000 unpaid. Because a sole trader has unlimited liability there is no company standing between the owner and that shortfall: the debt is the owner's own. The procedure in prospect is therefore bankruptcy, a declaration against the person, under which control of the owner's assets passes to an appointed official and assets held outside the business may be sold. Liquidation and administration do not apply, because there is no company to wind up or to rescue.

**Erongo Engineering.** Here there is a company, so both company procedures are available, and the choice between them turns on what the business is worth alive. Sold as separate assets the plant raises about N$2 000 000 against N$6 200 000 of debt, a shortfall of N$4 200 000. But forty skilled staff and two long-term mine contracts are worth something only while the business is running: a buyer would pay for a working engineering firm with contracts attached, and would pay nothing for them once the staff have gone and the contracts have been terminated.

Administration is the procedure that protects that value. The administrator takes over from the directors and normally works under protection from creditors enforcing their claims, which keeps the contracts intact while a buyer is sought or the debts are renegotiated.

**Recommendation.** Erongo's owners should seek administration rather than wait for a creditor to force a winding up. The decisive factor is the contracts: they are the only part of the business worth materially more inside it than outside it, and every week of uncertainty makes them harder to keep. The strongest argument against is cost and risk - the administrator's fees come out of the same money the creditors would share, and a rescue that fails ends in liquidation anyway with less left than there was.

So the recommendation is conditional on two things the directors should establish first: whether the mine contracts are profitable at the prices agreed, and whether the contracts can survive a change of ownership rather than being terminated by it. If the contracts are loss-making, or cannot be transferred, administration only postpones liquidation and consumes money on the way, and the better course is to move to liquidation directly.
marking_guidance: Both businesses must be analysed before the recommendation is made.
Judgement: a recommendation for Erongo's owners is required.
Context: must use the ownership form of each business and Erongo's staff and mine contracts.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be the value the contracts hold only while the business trades.
Counterargument: must address the administrator's costs and the risk of a failed rescue.
Condition: must state what would reverse the recommendation.
